title: Week 4 · Lesson 10: Endocrine Pathophysiology — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 4 — Lesson 10: Endocrine Pathophysiology

FNP-level goal

Use hormone physiology to explain presentation, interpret patterns rather than isolated laboratory values, identify dangerous metabolic or endocrine decompensation, and choose the appropriate outpatient, expedited, or emergency disposition.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain insulin, glucagon, and the mechanisms of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
  • Recognize hyperglycemic emergencies, including why potassium may be misleading in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
  • Interpret common thyroid patterns using the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis.
  • Connect adrenal cortisol and aldosterone physiology to hypotension, sodium, potassium, and adrenal crisis.
  • Build a focused differential and initial diagnostic plan for common endocrine presentations.

Part 1 — The clinical endocrine framework

Hormones are chemical signals. A useful clinical chain is: gland → hormone → receptor response → physiologic effect → feedback → symptoms when the system fails. A laboratory result only becomes useful when it is interpreted in that chain and in the patient’s clinical context.

Most endocrine axes use negative feedback. When the final hormone is adequate, upstream signaling falls; when the target gland fails, upstream drive often rises. This pattern helps distinguish a primary gland problem from a central pituitary or hypothalamic problem.

Part 2 — Glucose homeostasis

After a meal, rising glucose stimulates pancreatic beta cells to release insulin. Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage in muscle and adipose tissue and suppresses hepatic glucose production. During fasting, glucagon promotes hepatic glycogen breakdown and glucose production. In short: insulin stores fuel; glucagon mobilizes fuel.

Part 3 — Type 1 versus type 2 diabetes

Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune beta-cell destruction and severe insulin deficiency. Without enough insulin, tissues cannot appropriately use or store glucose. Lipolysis increases, the liver produces ketones, and DKA can develop.

Type 2 diabetes begins primarily with insulin resistance. The pancreas may initially compensate with higher insulin output, but progressive beta-cell dysfunction eventually makes insulin secretion inadequate for the body’s needs. Visceral adiposity, inflammatory signaling, and excess free fatty acids contribute to insulin resistance.

Do not reduce type 2 diabetes to “the patient does not make insulin.” Early in the disease, many patients make substantial insulin but cannot respond to it normally.

Part 4 — Why hyperglycemia causes polyuria and polydipsia

When filtered glucose exceeds renal reabsorptive capacity, glucose remains in the urine. Glucose retains water in the tubular lumen: hyperglycemia → glucosuria → osmotic diuresis → polyuria → water loss → polydipsia. Weight loss, fatigue, recurrent infections, and blurred vision should be connected to this metabolic process rather than memorized as an unrelated list.

Part 5 — DKA: mechanism and FNP disposition

Severe insulin deficiency causes hyperglycemia and also removes restraint on lipolysis. Free fatty acids reach the liver, ketone production rises, and metabolic acidosis develops. At the same time, glucosuria causes marked fluid and electrolyte loss. The core pattern is hyperglycemia + ketosis + metabolic acidosis + dehydration.

DKA is not a routine outpatient hyperglycemia visit. Vomiting, abdominal pain, tachypnea or deep breathing, dehydration, altered mental status, significant ketones, or suspected acidosis require urgent emergency evaluation and monitored treatment.

Part 6 — Potassium in DKA

A patient with DKA may have a normal or elevated serum potassium while still having severe total-body potassium depletion. Insulin deficiency and acidosis shift potassium out of cells, while osmotic diuresis and vomiting cause ongoing losses. When insulin and volume are corrected, serum potassium can fall rapidly. Therefore potassium and acid-base status are safety-critical parts of acute assessment; do not infer total-body stores from a single initial serum potassium value.

Part 7 — Chronic hyperglycemia: think beyond glucose

Persistent hyperglycemia contributes to microvascular injury involving the eyes, kidneys, and nerves, as well as macrovascular atherosclerotic disease. A patient with diabetes should trigger integrated thinking about blood pressure, lipids, kidney disease, cardiovascular risk, neuropathic symptoms, and albuminuria—not simply a glucose number.

Part 8 — Thyroid axis and pattern recognition

The thyroid axis is hypothalamus (TRH) → pituitary (TSH) → thyroid (T4/T3). Thyroid hormone feeds back to suppress TRH and TSH. T4 is produced in greater quantity; T3 has greater biologic activity, much of which is generated by peripheral conversion.

In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid fails: free T4 falls and the pituitary responds with high TSH. Typical physiology is reduced metabolic activity, which can present with fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, weight gain, bradycardia, and slowed cognition.

In primary hyperthyroidism, thyroid hormone is excessive: TSH is suppressed and free T4 and/or T3 is elevated. Increased metabolic and adrenergic activity can produce heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, palpitations, anxiety, and frequent bowel movements. New atrial fibrillation should prompt consideration of thyroid disease among the differential.

Part 9 — Primary versus central thyroid disease

Low free T4 does not always mean TSH will be high. In central hypothyroidism, the pituitary or hypothalamic signal is inadequate, so TSH can be low or inappropriately normal despite low free T4. Always ask: where is the failed step in the axis?

Part 10 — Adrenal physiology

The adrenal cortex produces cortisol and aldosterone. Cortisol is regulated through CRH → ACTH → cortisol and supports stress responses, glucose availability, vascular responsiveness, and immune regulation. Aldosterone links endocrine and renal physiology by promoting sodium retention and potassium secretion.

In primary adrenal insufficiency, the adrenal cortex fails. Cortisol falls, ACTH rises, and aldosterone may also be deficient. The resulting pattern can include fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, volume depletion, hyponatremia tendency, and hyperkalemia tendency. Increased ACTH-related signaling can contribute to hyperpigmentation.

Part 11 — Adrenal crisis is an emergency

Severe illness, injury, surgery, vomiting, or interrupted replacement therapy can precipitate adrenal crisis in a vulnerable patient. Concerning findings include hypotension or shock, severe weakness, vomiting or diarrhea, abdominal/back/leg pain, confusion, hypoglycemia, and loss of consciousness. This requires emergency treatment rather than outpatient observation.

Part 12 — Focused FNP diagnostic reasoning

For hyperglycemia, match testing to the presentation: chronic glycemic assessment, renal function and electrolytes, and—when acutely ill—ketones and acid-base evaluation. For thyroid concerns, interpret TSH with free T4 rather than treating a single value as a diagnosis. For suspected adrenal insufficiency, assess hemodynamic stability, electrolytes, glucose, medication history, and the timing of illness; unstable patients need emergency escalation.

Testing should answer a clinical question. Do not delay emergency care in an unstable patient simply to complete an outpatient endocrine workup.

Case 1 — Hyperglycemia with vomiting

A 23-year-old with diabetes has vomiting, abdominal pain, tachypnea, dehydration, and positive ketones. The reasoning chain is insulin deficiency → lipolysis → ketones → metabolic acidosis plus osmotic diuresis. The appropriate decision is emergency evaluation for a hyperglycemic crisis, including monitored electrolytes and acid-base status.

Case 2 — Fatigue and abnormal thyroid tests

A 48-year-old reports fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, dry skin, and weight gain. TSH is elevated and free T4 is low. This is the expected negative-feedback pattern of primary hypothyroidism: the pituitary is increasing TSH because the thyroid is failing to produce sufficient hormone.

Case 3 — Hypotension in a patient with adrenal disease

A patient with known adrenal insufficiency develops vomiting, profound weakness, confusion, and hypotension during an acute infection. This is not a routine medication refill issue. Stress-related cortisol deficiency can cause adrenal crisis and requires emergency care.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Identify the axis: glucose/insulin, thyroid, or adrenal.
  2. Explain the mechanism: deficiency, resistance, excess, or failed feedback.
  3. Link it to the presentation and key complications.
  4. Interpret laboratory patterns together, not in isolation.
  5. Screen for connected organ risk: kidney, cardiovascular, neurologic, and electrolyte effects.
  6. Decide disposition: stable outpatient evaluation, expedited specialty input, or emergency care.

High-Yield Summary

Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune beta-cell destruction → insulin deficiency → ketosis/DKA risk.
Type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance + progressive beta-cell dysfunction.
DKA: hyperglycemia + ketosis + metabolic acidosis + dehydration; initial serum potassium can mask total-body depletion.
Primary hypothyroidism: TSH high, free T4 low.
Primary hyperthyroidism: TSH low, free T4/T3 high.
Primary adrenal insufficiency: cortisol low, ACTH high; aldosterone deficiency can produce volume depletion and hyperkalemia.
Adrenal crisis: instability, vomiting, confusion, or shock requires emergency evaluation.

Extended Clinical Reasoning — From Mechanism to Decision

This extension builds on Parts 1–12. Work through each mechanism before memorizing the disease label. For every patient, separate three decisions: which hormonal process is abnormal, whether the patient is currently unstable, and which investigation or intervention should occur next. A plausible endocrine diagnosis does not exclude infection, cardiovascular disease, medication toxicity, or another concurrent process.

Part 13 — Receptors Explain Resistance and Delayed Effects

Peptide hormones such as insulin bind cell-surface receptors and activate intracellular signaling. Insulin signaling promotes movement of GLUT4 transporters to the surface of skeletal muscle and adipose cells, allowing greater glucose uptake. In insulin resistance, the signal becomes less effective: a given insulin concentration produces less metabolic response. This is different from an absolute lack of the hormone.

Steroid hormones and thyroid hormone act substantially through intracellular receptors that alter gene expression. Their effects often develop and resolve over longer intervals. This helps explain why symptom improvement may lag behind treatment and why repeating a hormone measurement immediately after a dose change may be misleading. Not all tissues require insulin to take up glucose: brain and red-cell glucose uptake is largely insulin-independent. Severe insulin deficiency is therefore not a literal inability of every cell to access glucose.

Part 14 — The Liver Is Central to Hyperglycemia

Muscle resistance reduces post-meal glucose disposal, but the liver also contributes by continuing glucose production when insulin should suppress it. Adipose insulin resistance increases release of fatty acids, adding substrate and signaling that worsen metabolic dysfunction. Beta cells initially compensate, then may become unable to meet demand.

This creates a reinforcing cycle: excess hepatic glucose output plus reduced peripheral disposal raises glucose; sustained metabolic stress further impairs beta-cell function. Treatment mechanisms make more sense when linked to the liver, muscle, adipose tissue, pancreas, kidney, and gut rather than to a single glucose number.

Part 15 — Diabetes Classification Requires Context

Do not classify diabetes solely from age or body size. Autoimmune diabetes can first appear in adulthood, and people with type 2 diabetes can develop ketosis during severe illness. Consider tempo, unintentional weight loss, ketosis, personal or family autoimmune disease, medication exposure, pancreatic disease, and the course after presentation.

When classification is uncertain, islet autoantibodies and appropriately interpreted C-peptide may help with specialist input. C-peptide reflects endogenous insulin secretion, but its meaning depends on concurrent glucose, kidney function, illness, and treatment context. These tests must not delay insulin or emergency assessment when clinical insulin deficiency is apparent. Pregnancy-related diabetes uses a separate diagnostic framework.

Part 16 — Diagnosing Diabetes Versus Measuring Control

For nonpregnant patients, diagnostic thresholds include laboratory A1c at least 6.5%, fasting plasma glucose at least 126 mg/dL, or two-hour glucose at least 200 mg/dL during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test. Random plasma glucose at least 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms or a hyperglycemic crisis can establish the diagnosis. Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, confirm an abnormal result with repeat or additional diagnostic testing.

Diagnosis and a treatment target are different decisions. A diagnostic threshold identifies disease; the appropriate treatment goal depends on age, comorbidities, hypoglycemia risk, life expectancy, and preferences. Do not mistake a single home-meter reading for a complete laboratory diagnostic evaluation.

Part 17 — When A1c and Glucose Disagree

A1c depends on both glucose exposure and red-cell biology. Recent transfusion, hemolysis, some anemias, hemoglobin variants, pregnancy, and advanced kidney disease can distort interpretation. A1c also averages exposure and may conceal alternating hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia.

If symptoms or measured glucose conflict with A1c, investigate the discrepancy instead of intensifying treatment automatically. Ask about bleeding, transfusion, erythropoietin, and red-cell disorders; review glucose patterns and assay limitations. A reassuring average does not exclude dangerous glucose excursions or rapidly developing insulin deficiency.

Part 18 — DKA and HHS: Different Dominant Mechanisms

DKA is driven by insufficient insulin to restrain ketogenesis, producing ketones and metabolic acidosis. In hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS), enough insulin activity may remain to limit ketogenesis, but not enough to prevent profound hyperglycemia, water loss, and hyperosmolality. Neurologic dysfunction can accompany severe hyperosmolar dehydration.

These syndromes overlap and neither is exclusive to one diabetes type. Both require monitored emergency care. Infection, interrupted therapy, infarction, and medication effects can precipitate crisis. Assess the precipitant as well as the metabolic abnormality.

Part 19 — Euglycemic DKA and Ketone Testing

DKA can occur without marked glucose elevation, particularly with SGLT2 inhibitor exposure, reduced intake, or pregnancy. Nausea, abdominal pain, deep breathing, or systemic illness should not be dismissed because glucose is only modestly elevated. Evaluate ketones and acid-base status when the clinical pattern suggests it.

Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate directly measures the predominant ketone in DKA. Urine ketone tests measure a different ketone and may lag behind clinical changes. Emergency treatment integrates fluids, insulin, electrolytes, and precipitant management with repeated monitoring; it is not simply a rapid glucose-lowering exercise.

Part 20 — Refine the Potassium Explanation

The key distinction is concentration versus total-body content. Insulin deficiency and hypertonicity promote extracellular potassium shifts, while urinary losses deplete stores. Acidemia may contribute, but organic ketoacidosis does not produce a predictable one-for-one potassium shift. Do not calculate potassium needs from pH alone.

As insulin action returns, potassium moves into cells. Volume restoration and changing kidney function further alter measured potassium. A low presenting potassium is particularly concerning because treatment may lower it further. Monitored protocols coordinate potassium replacement and insulin timing; unmonitored insulin correction is unsafe in suspected crisis.

Part 21 — Hypoglycemia: The Opposite Emergency

Insulin and insulin secretagogues can lower glucose below physiologic need, especially with missed meals, exercise, alcohol, impaired kidney clearance, or dosing errors. Adrenergic symptoms include tremor, sweating, palpitations, and hunger. Neuroglycopenia produces confusion, behavior change, seizure, or loss of consciousness.

An alert patient able to swallow can receive rapidly absorbed carbohydrate with prompt reassessment according to the established action plan. Altered consciousness requires emergency assistance and appropriate rescue therapy; do not give food or liquid orally to someone unable to swallow safely. After recovery, determine the cause and recurrence risk rather than treating the episode as closed.

Part 22 — Connect Complications to Mechanisms

Chronic hyperglycemia promotes glycation, oxidative stress, and endothelial injury. Glomerular damage may cause albuminuria and declining filtration; retinal microvascular injury threatens vision; peripheral and autonomic nerve injury may impair sensation, gastric motility, or orthostatic responses.

Loss of foot sensation plus pressure injury, poor circulation, and impaired healing can create an ulcer the patient does not feel. FNP assessment therefore includes the feet, vascular risk, kidney measures, eye evaluation, and symptoms of neuropathy. Albuminuria supports kidney injury but is not automatically proof that diabetes is its only cause.

Part 23 — Thyrotoxicosis Is Not Always Overproduction

Thyrotoxicosis means excessive thyroid-hormone action from any cause. Hyperthyroidism specifically means increased gland production. Graves disease stimulates production through TSH-receptor antibodies; autonomous nodules produce hormone independently. Thyroiditis can release stored hormone from an injured gland without increased synthesis.

This difference changes treatment. A drug that blocks new hormone synthesis does not directly stop leakage of preformed hormone from thyroiditis. History of neck pain, recent pregnancy, medication exposure, goiter, eye findings, and disease trajectory helps guide cause-specific evaluation.

Part 24 — Interpret Thyroid Patterns as Pairs

  • High TSH plus low free T4: overt primary hypothyroidism.
  • High TSH plus normal free T4: a subclinical pattern requiring context and often confirmation.
  • Low TSH plus elevated free T4 and/or T3: thyrotoxicosis; determine its cause.
  • Low TSH plus normal free hormones: possible subclinical hyperthyroidism, transient suppression, drug effect, or other context-dependent explanation.
  • Low free T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH: consider central disease, severe illness, and confounders.

Subclinical is a laboratory description, not proof that treatment is always needed or never needed. Persistence, degree of abnormality, symptoms, cardiac and skeletal risks, pregnancy, and age influence the decision.

Part 25 — Thyroid Testing Traps

Acute illness can alter thyroid tests without a primary thyroid disorder. Biotin can interfere with some assays and create misleading results. Ask about supplements, amiodarone, lithium, glucocorticoids, and thyroid products, and communicate with the laboratory when results are discordant. Follow assay-specific guidance about withholding biotin rather than assuming one interval works for every dose and assay.

Ultrasound evaluates structure, not hormone production. An abnormal TSH alone does not automatically require ultrasound; a palpable nodule, enlargement, or structural concern raises a different question. Separate biochemical dysfunction from structural disease.

Part 26 — Thyroid Management Through Physiology

Levothyroxine replaces deficient hormone. Absorption, food timing, iron or calcium supplements, adherence, and medication interactions affect response. In primary hypothyroidism, TSH generally helps guide follow-up after enough time for equilibration. In central hypothyroidism, TSH is not a reliable replacement target.

When pituitary disease or adrenal insufficiency is suspected, assess cortisol safety before starting thyroid replacement because increasing metabolic demand can unmask adrenal crisis. Pregnancy, coronary disease, and frailty require individualized management. A beta blocker may reduce adrenergic symptoms in appropriate thyrotoxic patients, but it does not establish the cause or correct every mechanism.

Part 27 — Thyroid Emergencies Are Clinical Syndromes

Thyroid storm involves severe systemic decompensation in a thyrotoxic patient, potentially including fever, marked tachycardia or arrhythmia, delirium, gastrointestinal symptoms, and heart failure. Myxedema coma refers to severe decompensated hypothyroidism; hypothermia, impaired ventilation, altered mentation, and circulatory compromise are concerning even without literal coma.

Neither diagnosis is made from the height of a hormone value alone. Recognize instability, arrange emergency care, and evaluate triggers such as infection or medication interruption. These patients require monitored multidisciplinary treatment.

Part 28 — Primary Versus Central Adrenal Insufficiency

In primary disease, adrenal damage can reduce both cortisol and aldosterone. In central disease, inadequate ACTH reduces cortisol, but aldosterone is often relatively preserved because it is regulated mainly by RAAS and potassium. Hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation are therefore less typical in central disease.

Hyponatremia can still occur with cortisol deficiency because impaired water excretion and increased vasopressin activity affect sodium concentration. A normal potassium does not exclude adrenal insufficiency. Interpret electrolytes together with blood pressure, symptoms, medication history, and axis localization.

Part 29 — Testing the Adrenal Axis Safely

In a stable patient, appropriately timed cortisol and ACTH can help distinguish inadequate cortisol production from altered central drive. ACTH stimulation testing may be needed, with interpretation depending on assay and clinical circumstances. A random cortisol result should not be treated as universally diagnostic.

In suspected adrenal crisis, treatment must not wait for confirmatory results. If samples can be drawn immediately without delaying care, they may help later interpretation. Emergency glucocorticoid treatment and resuscitation take priority. Recent-onset central disease can complicate stimulation-test interpretation and warrants specialist guidance.

Part 30 — Exogenous Steroids Can Suppress the Axis

Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress hypothalamic and pituitary drive. After sufficient exposure, abrupt withdrawal may leave endogenous cortisol production unable to meet demand. Risk depends on dose, duration, potency, route, and interacting drugs; ask about injections, inhaled and topical preparations as well as oral therapy.

Do not use one universal taper. Coordinate a patient-specific plan and reassessment. Patients at risk need clear illness instructions, particularly when vomiting prevents oral medication absorption. Hemodynamic instability after recent steroid exposure should prompt consideration of adrenal crisis.

Part 31 — Cortisol Excess: A Pattern, Not One Symptom

Cortisol excess can cause insulin resistance, hypertension, muscle protein breakdown, skin fragility, osteoporosis, and infection susceptibility. Weight gain alone is nonspecific; proximal weakness, easy bruising, wide violaceous striae, and progressive multisystem findings increase concern.

First review exogenous steroid exposure. Endogenous Cushing syndrome requires appropriately selected biochemical evaluation, often with specialist involvement, rather than interpretation of an isolated random cortisol. Cushing disease specifically refers to a pituitary ACTH-producing cause and is not interchangeable with every cause of cortisol excess.

Part 32 — Aldosterone and Secondary Hypertension

Excess aldosterone enhances sodium reabsorption and potassium and hydrogen-ion secretion. This can produce hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis, but many affected patients have normal potassium. Resistant hypertension or a suggestive clinical pattern should prompt consideration beyond essential hypertension.

An aldosterone-renin assessment requires attention to medications, potassium status, sampling conditions, and the laboratory method. A ratio alone is not the entire diagnosis. Coordinate interpretation and subsequent testing; do not discontinue necessary cardiovascular drugs indiscriminately to obtain a screening sample.

Part 33 — Polyuria: Glucose, Water, or Frequency?

Clarify whether the patient produces a large urine volume or merely voids often. Dysuria with small frequent voids differs from true polyuria. With large-volume urine, consider glucose-driven osmotic diuresis, diuretic use, primary polydipsia, and impaired vasopressin secretion or action.

Serum sodium, glucose, volume status, and urine concentration help frame the mechanism. A water-balance disorder can cause dangerous sodium abnormalities. Specialized deprivation or stimulation testing requires supervision; patients should not attempt fluid deprivation at home.

Part 34 — Worked Case: Modest Glucose, Serious Illness

A patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor has poor intake, vomiting, abdominal pain, and deep breathing. Glucose is 182 mg/dL. The reassuring-looking glucose does not resolve the presentation. Medication context and symptoms justify urgent assessment for ketones, acidosis, dehydration, and other acute causes.

Decision: emergency evaluation for possible euglycemic DKA. Trap: assuming DKA requires extreme glucose. Transferable reasoning: follow the physiologic syndrome rather than a single laboratory threshold.

Part 35 — Worked Case: Low T4 Without High TSH

A patient has fatigue, low free T4, non-elevated TSH, headaches, and new visual symptoms. Central disease must be considered along with testing confounders. Other pituitary functions, especially cortisol, matter before replacement decisions.

Decision: evaluate the pituitary pattern and visual urgency; sudden severe headache or acute visual loss requires emergency assessment. Trap: calling the thyroid normal because TSH falls within the laboratory range.

Part 36 — Worked Case: Steroid Withdrawal and Shock

A patient recently stopped prolonged glucocorticoid treatment and now has infection, vomiting, profound weakness, and hypotension. The differential includes sepsis, volume depletion, and adrenal crisis; more than one may be present.

Decision: emergency resuscitation and prompt treatment of suspected cortisol deficiency without awaiting outpatient confirmation. Trap: excluding adrenal crisis because potassium is normal. Central suppression may preserve aldosterone.

Part 37 — Worked Case: Which Thyroid Process?

A patient has palpitations, weight loss, suppressed TSH, and high free T4. These establish a thyrotoxic pattern, not its cause. Ask about thyroid pain, recent pregnancy, eye findings, supplements, prescribed thyroid hormone, and relevant drugs. Focused antibodies or other cause-specific testing may follow.

Decision: assess severity, identify the mechanism, and choose appropriate treatment. Trap: assuming every thyrotoxic patient has Graves disease and will benefit from the same medication.

Extended Review — Questions to Explain Aloud

  1. Why can a patient have substantial insulin secretion and still develop type 2 diabetes?
  2. Why can a normal-looking glucose fail to exclude DKA?
  3. Why does serum potassium not measure total-body potassium stores?
  4. What differentiates hormone overproduction from release of stored hormone?
  5. Why might low free T4 coexist with a normal TSH?
  6. Why may steroid-induced adrenal insufficiency occur without hyperkalemia?
  7. Which symptoms require emergency evaluation before the endocrine diagnosis is confirmed?

Explain each answer through the affected axis, mechanism, findings, and next action. The existing lesson quiz remains available; these prompts extend understanding without replacing its questions or changing recorded progress.

Scope: This is an expanded pathophysiology and clinical-reasoning lesson. Detailed prescribing regimens belong in the pharmacology curriculum. Apply current disease-specific guidance and patient-specific assessment in practice.
